However, there is no consensus on carbon footprint accounting and species Discrepancy of the e-waste recycling process in China. This paper first explores the accounting method for carbon footprint in the e-waste Dismantling process. After that, the carbon footprint inventory of dismantling process is produced by finely matching the daily electricity consumption of key energy-using facilities and the daily dismantling volume of five types of e-waste. Finally, combining the changes in the annual dismantling volume and the proportion of e-waste dismantling types, it is found that inter-annual change of carbon footprint is not only closely related to the trend of total dismantling volume that first increases and then stabilizes from 2013 to 2020, but also due to the gradual increase in the industry’s average carbon emissions of Dismantling a single unit from 1.2513 kgCO /unit to 1.3335 k gCO /unit. The results show that there are signifi- 2 2 cant differences in the carbon emission factors of five types of e-waste products. Refrigerators have a higher carbon emission factor due to the complex dismantling process and higher energy consumption, and conversely, TVs have a lower carbon emission factor. Carbon footprint from e-waste dismantling process in China show a trend of "regional agglomeration + single point prominence". Highlights • Calculate the carbon emission factors of five types of e-waste dismantling process combining field research. • Comparatively analyze the carbon footprint of different varieties and segments of e-waste dismantling process. • Deeply analyze the scale and distribution of carbon footprint within China’s e-waste dismantling industry. JSON: Name: field_based_bottom_up_ewaste_accounting Title: Field-based bottom-up emission-factor accounting and spatial–temporal decomposition for the carbon footprint of e-waste dismantling in China Short Hypothesis: Metered, facility-level electricity and fossil-fuel consumption matched to daily, product-level dismantling throughput produces product-specific dismantling emission factors that explain at least 90% of cross-enterprise variance and enable provincial-level carbon footprint estimates with mean absolute percentage error ≤ 10% versus audited totals. Related Work: Existing approaches to quantify greenhouse-gas emissions from e-waste combine three dominant paradigms: top-down emission-factor inventories (IPCC-style national or grid-average factors), life-cycle assessment (LCA) studies that estimate cradle-to-grave impacts using material and process models, and limited field studies targeting specific streams (e.g., refrigerant recovery). Top-down inventories offer broad coverage but use coarse activity data and grid averages that obscure dismantling-segment heterogeneity. LCA studies provide product-level detail but often rely on literature assumptions or secondary process data and do not capture operational variability in dismantling facilities. Prior field research focuses on refrigerant or toxic exposures and rarely links high-frequency energy metering to daily dismantling throughput by product type. Unresolved issues include inconsistent system boundaries for the dismantling segment, lack of validated product-specific emission factors derived from operational facility data, limited temporal resolution, poor treatment of spatial variation in grid factors, and scarce uncertainty quantification when upscaling from sample facilities to provincial or national inventories. Abstract: This research develops and validates a field-based, bottom-up accounting pipeline that derives product-specific carbon emission factors for e-waste dismantling by matching metered facility energy use to daily dismantling throughput and then upscales results to provincial and national inventories with spatial–temporal decomposition of drivers. The pipeline uses facility-level electricity meters, fossil-fuel consumption logs, equipment-level segmentation (dismantling, crushing, dust control, transport, power, dining), and provincial grid emission factors to compute per-unit dismantling emissions for five common categories (TVs, refrigerators, washing machines, air conditioners, computers). Contributions are: (1) a standardized accounting protocol and uncertainty-aware estimator for dismantling emission factors; (2) a validation and cross-validation study across a stratified sample of enterprises to quantify representativeness; and (3) a spatial–temporal decomposition that attributes inter-annual and inter-provincial footprint changes to volume, product mix, and per-unit emission-factor shifts. Expected outcomes are validated emission factors, national-scale inventories with predictive error bounds, and identification of high-impact process segments and regions for mitigation and policy design. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Primary field dataset: daily metered electricity (kWh) and fuel consumption (L/ m3) for main facilities (dismantling benches, conveyors, shredders, dust collectors, compressors, forklifts, boilers, canteens) and daily dismantled unit counts by product subtype for N=40 enterprises stratified across 7 regions and 29 provinces for a 2018–2020 window; (2) provincial annual grid emission factors (tCO2/MWh) for 2013–2020; (3) official provincial annual dismantling volumes for 2013–2020; (4) third-party audit reports for M=8 enterprises for validation; (5) LCA reference database (e.g., ecoinvent) for baseline comparison. Baselines: (A) top-down IPCC/national-average EF scaling using provincial volumes; (B) LCA-derived per-unit dismantling estimates from literature; (C) Ba et al. style aggregate-factor approach. Metrics: enterprise-level R2 and RMSE between predicted and observed annual emissions; provincial-level MAPE and bias; coverage probability of 90% predictive intervals; decomposition share (%) of drivers (volume, product mix, per-unit EF); sensitivity indices (Sobol first-order) for energy components. Experimental setup: (i) Compute per-enterprise, per-product EF = (metered facility electricity × provincial grid EF + direct fuel combustion CO2) / units_dismantled; (ii) Cross-validate via leave-one-enterprise-out (LOEO) and 5-fold stratified by province; (iii) Ablation studies: A1 remove facility-level granularity (use aggregate electricity for enterprise); A2 use national grid EF instead of provincial; A3 collapse segments (treat dismantling+crushing as single segment); (iv) Upscaling strategies compared: S1 stratified extrapolation by enterprise type and region; S2 proportional scaling by provincial volumes; evaluate provincial MAPE and coverage vs audit reports; (v) Statistical tests: paired t-test for baseline vs proposed MAE differences, bootstrap (10,000 resamples) to generate 95% CIs; (vi) Uncertainty quantification: propagate meter noise (±5%), grid EF uncertainty, and throughput reporting error via Monte Carlo (10,000 draws) to generate predictive intervals. Expected comparisons: proposed pipeline vs baselines on R2, RMSE, provincial MAPE, and PI coverage. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Data completeness and quality: gaps, timestamp misalignment between metered energy and dismantling throughput, or misreported unit counts may bias EF estimates; 2) Sample bias: the study relies on formally licensed enterprises and may not represent informal dismantling operations; 3) Representativeness: N=40 enterprises may be insufficient to capture full technological and managerial heterogeneity, especially for small workshops; 4) Grid-factor dynamics: provincial grid emission factors change annually and spatially; using average factors introduces temporal mismatch error when metered data lack matching timestamps; 5) Unobserved emissions: refrigerant fugitive emissions, solvent releases, and off-site processes are not captured if not metered or reported, leading to underestimation of total climate impact; 6) Scaling uncertainty: upscaling from sampled enterprises to provincial/national inventories amplifies sampling and stratification errors; 7) Policy and market shifts: subsidy changes or rapid shifts in product mix during the study period limit historical extrapolation; 8) Computational limits: Monte Carlo uncertainty propagation and Sobol sensitivity for large upscaling scenarios require moderate compute resources; 9) Generalization: the method and emission factors derived for China may not transfer to countries with different energy mixes, regulatory frameworks, or informal-sector prevalence.
